tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

`src/glob.js` must export `compile`, `isMatch`, `filter` and the error class `GlobError`. `compile(pattern, options)` returns a function that reports whether a whole path matches; `isMatch(path, pattern, options)` is the one-shot form, and `filter(paths, pattern, options)` keeps the matching paths in their original order without removing duplicates. Paths are separated by `/` and a pattern is anchored at both ends. Within one segment, `*` matches any run of characters other than `/`, including none, and `?` matches exactly one character other than `/`; a run of several `*` in a segment behaves as one.

A segment that is exactly `**` matches zero or more whole segments, so `a/**/b` matches `a/b`, `a/x/b` and `a/x/y/b` but not `a/b/c`, `**/a` matches `a` and `x/y/a`, `a/**` matches `a` as well as `a/b/c`, and adjacent `**` segments collapse into one. A bracket expression matches one character: `[abc]` and ranges such as `[a-c]` match a listed character, while `[!...]` and `[^...]` match one character that is neither `/` nor listed. A `]` written immediately after the opening bracket, or after the negation mark, is a literal `]`, a `-` at either end of the list is a literal `-`, and a backslash inside the brackets escapes the next character. Outside brackets a backslash also removes the special meaning of the next character, so `\*` matches a literal asterisk. Characters that are special to regular expressions but not to globs, such as `.`, `+`, `(` and `$`, always stand for themselves.

A path segment that begins with `.` is matched only by a pattern segment that itself begins with a literal `.` (optionally written as `\.`): `*`, `?`, `**` and a bracket expression all refuse a leading dot, so `*` does not match `.x`, `**/y` does not match `.x/y`, and `[.]x` does not match `.x`, while `.*` does. `options.dot` set to true removes that restriction everywhere. `options.nocase` set to true makes matching case-insensitive. Neither option changes anything else.

Every failure throws `GlobError`, and a positional one carries the 0-based `index` into the pattern where the fault starts: `unterminated character class` (index of the opening bracket), `trailing backslash` (index of the backslash), and `path separator in character class` (index of the `/`). An empty pattern (`pattern must not be empty`) and a non-string pattern (`pattern must be a string`) are rejected without an index, as are a non-string path (`path must be a string`) and a non-array first argument to `filter` (`paths must be an array`). Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.\n\n`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.\n\n`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. goal.objective:
Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.

`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The segments are then joined with single slashes and the result normalized, so joining can itself raise `'ESCAPE'`.

`relative(from, to)` returns the relative path that leads from the first location to the second. Both arguments must be absolute, otherwise it throws `'NOT_ABSOLUTE'` with message `both paths must be absolute`. Both are normalized first, so an escaping argument raises `'ESCAPE'`. The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. Two equal paths give the empty string. The result is always relative, always already normalized, and joining it back onto `from` (using `.` in place of the empty string) reproduces `to`.
